newsitem.title: FRANCE: MEPs in confusion over seaweed.
newsitem.headline: MEPs in confusion over seaweed.

text.p: The European Parliament was thrown into confusion on Wednesday by a seaweed-based food additive produced in the Philippines.

Technical problems with several voting machines meant that MEPs ended up approving, instead of rejecting, a European Commission proposal to include processed eucheuma seaweed (PES) in the 1995 EU directive on permitted food additives.
The result means that PES, a product which can contain residues of heavy metals and is currently only used in pet food in Europe, can now be used in human foodstuffs.

The outcome of the vote -- two MEPs too few to reject the Commission proposal -- was met with howls of dismay by deputies, protesting that their machines had not worked and that chairwoman Nicole Pery was going too fast.
Rapporteur Karin Riis-Jorgensen, a Danish Liberal, told Reuters she and several other MEPs would formally request a revote on Thursday.
Riis-Jorgensen has been campaigning since last November to have PES labelled differently from an already permitted food additive made from seaweed.
Carageenan, as it is know, is a highly refined product used mainly in desserts and meat and is identified by the additive number E407.

The Commission's proposal -- COM(95)177 -- recommends giving PES the E number E407a and calling it "alternatively refined carrageenan" or ARC, a position which has been welcomed by the government in Manila.
"The measure will end more than five years of exclusion of this Philippine product in the EU market," said President Ramos in a letter to the European Parliament in February.

After protests from the Parliament's environment committee, European carrageenan producers and the European Bureau of Consumer Unions (BEUC), MEPs said in their first reading of the proposal in March that carageenan and PES were two different products and should be labelled distinctly in the interests of European consumers.
Eu ministers ignored Parliament's demand that PES keep its name and bear the E-number 408 to prevent any confusion, hence the reintroduction of the request at the second reading on Wednesday.
If Wednesday's voting muddle is not rectified on Thursday, the implications for Euroepan consumers will be serious, Riis-Jorgensen said.
"You might be confused and use a less refined product instead of a better one, so if you are allergic you might have problems," she said.

The Irish Seaweed Industry Organisation wrote to Irish Liberal MEP Pat Cox last autumn to say any confusion between the two additives would damage carageenan's reputation amongst food producers and result in unfair competition.
